thread.title: Microsoft: How The Acquisition Of GitHub Reflects Where The Modern Corporation Is Going - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) | Seeking Alpha

author: John M. Mason
title: Microsoft: How The Acquisition Of GitHub Reflects Where The Modern Corporation Is Going - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Less than a month ago, I wrote a post titled " Apple, the Epitome of Where the Modern Corporation is Going ." This piece focused almost solely on Apple, Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and what distinguished it from other corporations so that it could be presented as an example of where the modern corporation is going.
Soon after, I followed this up with another post titled " Apple: Where the Modern Corporation is Going--II ." The example of Apple was expanded with an illustration of how Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN ) also was showing traits exhibited by Apple that fit into the definition of the modern corporation I was describing.
Today, I would like to bring in a third example, Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT ) to exhibit how the modern corporation is evolving.
The specific reason for the timing of this post is the just announced acquisition Microsoft is making of the online code-sharing platform GitHub. The acquisition is for $7.5 billion.
Let me just note before delving deeper into this transition that Microsoft chief executive officer, Satya Nadella, has just entered his fifth year in this position and is still taking the company through a transition begun after Mr. Nadella took over from former CEO Steve Ballmer.
A very new culture has been evolving at Microsoft, one being the move by Mr. Nadella into "open source" technology, something that Mr. Ballmer was strongly opposed to.
The acquisition of GitHub, which works with open source software developers, is just another example of how Mr. Nadella has moved Microsoft toward a more open platform that can include many creators and competitors.
Furthermore, let me add the point that Microsoft has not had a return on shareholders' equity of less than 30 percent since 2010, coming out of the Great Recession.
One can argue very strongly that Microsoft has what is called a sustainable competitive advantage in the marketplace, a situation that can be exploited without doing too much else for several years.
The difficulty faced by corporate management in such a situation is how to evolve the corporation so as to continue to sustain the company's performance, especially in an industry that is moving along as rapidly as is the computer/Internet/software space.
The rapidly changing nature of this space is captured, I believe, in the fact that when Microsoft is written about, like in the current case of the acquisition of GitHub, the writers don't picture Microsoft as just a software firm, or Apple as part of the computer peripherals industry, of Amazon as part of the Internet community. And, the same goes for Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ).
And, these firms are not tossed into the category called conglomerates. Conglomerates are generally pictured as a business that runs a portfolio of companies, not necessarily producing the same products or services, but run under the assumption that the management can allocate resources among the members of the total organization better than the stock market can.
This ability to allocate resources within the portfolio produces excess returns over the market to justify the banding together of the distinct entities in such a combination.
Perhaps the best term that is used to describe how these new "modern" corporations are put together is the word "network." That is, there is something implicit in the combination of activities that these modern corporations put together that "bind" things together, even if it does not look, on the surface, like there is something in common in the things brought together.
Amazon.com has proven to be very adept at this practice. As a consequence, these new "modern" corporations can build, not only to a scale but also to a scope that the legacy corporations or conglomerates were not able to do.
This is because, as I mentioned in the first post cited above that the new corporation is "a leader in the use of intangibles like intellectual property and brands relative to tangible goods."
Microsoft, in combining with GitHub, is "emphasizing its role as a provider of tools and cloud-based services for developers on all platforms-even those owned by the company's rivals," writes Dan Gallagher in the Wall Street Journal . This is building a community that is tied together by what Microsoft is offering… a network.
But, this is not totally new for Microsoft, as Jay Greene mentions in another article in the Wall Street Journal. This is how Microsoft counted on a community of developers to help it, in the 1990s, "build their applications for its windows operating system." And, the process was very, very successful.
GitHub is bringing 28 million developers along with the company.
The "use of intangibles" is very important in the new "modern" corporations and, used wisely, can bring all sorts of people and situations together to build larger and more diverse organizations. This is the new way. It has helped Microsoft move from being a PC-dependent company to being a "credible cloud computing company."
But the new "modern" corporation is also adept at financial engineering. It not only builds through mergers and acquisitions but also using its cash extremely well.
Microsoft has around $130 billion in cash lying around. It uses that cash very well.
Note, however, that in the current purchase of GitHub, Microsoft is choosing to pay in shares. In essence, Microsoft is giving up about one percent of itself to the GitHub shareholders.
But, hold on. Mr. Greene writes explains "Microsoft intends to increase its stock repurchasing to offset within six months the shares paid for GitHub…." So, Microsoft is planning to "pay cash" for the company, but, at the same time, it will buy up its own shares, and, with a lesser number of shares around, it should be able to increase its return on shareholders' equity.
In addition, Mr. Greene goes on, "That strategy should help the sellers defer the tax impact of the transaction." It appears as if we have a win-win situation. GitHub still has many of the original founders and investors and a venture capital firm or two still to benefit from the transaction.
The bottom line is that almost everything related to this transaction is intangible, which was certainty not the case in terms of the "old" modern corporation.
The question for those that would like to become a "new" modern corporation is "how do I turn my 'tangibles' into something that is 'intangible'?" Maybe an answer comes for the field of Information Theory, which argues that everything is information, an intangible even the computer that you are reading this post on. The issue then becomes how do you translate this into actual business practice? More on this later.
